findings.text: The opening paragraph says plainly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. A newcomer can say what this is within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: There is a link to the next step at the top. The Next steps section gives the prerequisites, the clone command, ./setup.sh and a first command (athena ask "add a changelog"), so the reader knows exactly what to do.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself." and the Next steps section

findings.text: This is Athena's site, but almost all of the page describes another tool, firstmate: its states, exit codes and teardown rules. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to read past a lot of material that only matters if they care about firstmate.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the sections States of a piece of work, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: The main promise is a traceable commit with its cost and verdict, but the page never shows one. The example given is a read-only study, so the reader sees traceability of claims but not the change-making workflow they would install Athena for.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This link sits in the header and is addressed to the project owner. A newcomer may think it applies to them, or be unsure what the "proposals" are.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The body is packed with internal terms and IDs (places-held, exit 75, pending-close record, t1–t12, c1–c45). The glossary helps, but a first-time reader will struggle to follow the cards.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"; t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75"

findings.text: Several terms are defined twice, once in Start here and again in the Glossary. This makes an already long page longer without adding anything for the reader.
findings.source: "Words used first" ... "Each is defined here, and again in the Glossary at the end of the page."

findings.text: The page is open that nothing was run, only read. That builds trust, but it also tells the reader that the evidence comes from file headers, not observed behaviour.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The prerequisites are concrete. They do not say whether a paid model account is needed, or what a typical run costs, even though the page stresses cost tracking.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)."
